analysis.one_liner: Opens shipping routes to Hawaii, Alaska, and U.S. territories to competition when the Jones Act leaves them without it.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Jones Act exemption bill from a Hawaii Democrat and a Guam Republican was introduced in January 2025 and has sat in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law requires ships carrying goods between U.S. ports to be built in the United States, mostly U.S.-owned, and American-crewed. On routes to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories, few carriers meet those rules, so shippers face little competition and residents pay high freight rates that show up in the price of nearly everything. This bill would suspend those requirements on a route unless at least three independent carriers each already carry at least a fifth of its goods — meaning competition gets a chance exactly where it is missing today. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee, where it has stayed.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents and businesses of Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam, and other U.S. territories, who pay some of the country's highest shipping costs because a handful of Jones Act carriers face little competition on their routes. Opening those routes to foreign-built and foreign-crewed vessels would add competitors, and added competition on freight routes generally pushes shipping prices down — savings that flow into the cost of food, fuel, cars, and building materials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of Hawaii, Alaska, and U.S. territories

how_it_helps.text: On any noncontiguous route — a route touching Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, or a U.S. territory — the Jones Act's U.S.-built, U.S.-owned, and U.S.-crewed requirements would no longer apply, unless the route already has at least three independent operators each carrying 20% or more of its volume, in which case competition already exists and the exemption does not trigger.

Because most noncontiguous routes are served by fewer than three carriers, the exemption would apply precisely on the routes where shippers currently have the least choice, letting lower-cost vessels into the market.
Lower freight costs on island and Alaska routes would be passed through to consumers on a wide range of goods, since ocean shipping is the only practical way to move most cargo to these places.

analysis.who_pays: The small set of U.S. shipping companies that hold protected routes to Hawaii, Alaska, and the territories would face new competition and lose the premium rates a captive market allows. U.S. shipyards would lose the guaranteed orders that come from the requirement that Jones Act vessels be American-built, and American crews working those routes could see cargo shift to foreign-flagged, foreign-crewed ships.
analysis.who_pays_short: Jones Act ship operators and U.S. shipyards

drawbacks.text: Supporters of the Jones Act argue that requiring U.S.-built, U.S.-crewed ships preserves an American shipbuilding base and a pool of U.S. mariners that the military relies on to move supplies in a crisis; exempting the noncontiguous routes would move that cargo off U.S.-flag vessels.
American crews and U.S.-flag operators on island and Alaska routes could lose work to foreign-flagged ships, a real cost to a relatively small workforce even as consumers gain.
The exemption is conditional: if a route's carriers cross the three-operator threshold, the exemption disappears, which could complicate investment decisions for any new entrant.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of Americans in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories, the potential savings on freight are broad and concrete, because shipping costs are baked into nearly every price they pay. The costs fall on a concentrated group — a few shipping companies, the U.S. shipbuilding industry, and maritime crews — whose main argument is national security: that a protected merchant fleet is worth paying a premium for. That tradeoff is genuine, but it has historically been decided by the concentrated interests' influence in Congress rather than by the people paying the premium.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2025, sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, and then referred to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ed Case (D-HI) introduced the bill on January 23, 2025, joined by Rep. James Moylan (R-GU), whose district is among the noncontiguous trades the bill covers.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on January 23, 2025, and to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation on January 24, 2025.
The sponsor delivered introductory remarks on the measure on February 4, 2025.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — has been recorded since referral, with the Congress still in session.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the status quo holds: the small group of carriers with protected island and Alaska routes and the U.S. shipyards that build their vessels keep their guaranteed positions, while residents of Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and the territories keep paying Jones Act freight rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Jones Act carriers and shipyards, for now

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor is a Hawaii Democrat and the original cosponsor a Guam Republican, with one additional cosponsor from each party; no votes have been held to measure the broader split.

industries.industry: Jones Act shipping carriers serving Hawaii, Alaska, and the territories
industries.note: These carriers hold routes where the Jones Act rules leave them with little or no competition, allowing above-market freight rates. The exemption would open routes with fewer than three independent operators to new competitors, ending that protection.

The requirement that Jones Act vessels be built in U.S. yards guarantees domestic shipbuilders orders at prices well above world levels. Exempting the noncontiguous routes would allow foreign-built ships, shrinking that protected market.
They could enter U.S. island and Alaska routes for the first time, and the competition they bring is the mechanism by which freight costs for residents would fall.

industries.industry: American merchant mariners and U.S.-flag crewing on noncontiguous routes
industries.note: Crews could lose work as cargo shifts to foreign-crewed vessels, a real cost to a small workforce; consumers gain through lower shipping costs.

analysis.trajectory: Jones Act exemption bills have a long history of stalling in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, where maritime interests carry weight, and this one shows no committee action in its first year and only two cosponsors. Absent a large expansion of support, it is most likely to die without a hearing or vote when this Congress ends.
